cultivar: Mixed Indian, Chinese, Japanese and Taiwanese varietals; own JO selection
processing: Small-batch high-mountain teas, with withering and oxidation judged by sight, smell and touch rather than fixed timings. The range runs across the oxidation spectrum: the garden names blacks, greens and whites, and retailers also sell oolongs.
harvest_season: Early spring in March, spring from April to early May, a dormant spell in mid to late May, early summer from June to mid-July, summer to September, autumn in October and November, and a little in December.
appearance_dry: Long, wiry, well-made dark leaf with lighter tips in the black teas; the appearance changes with the style.
appearance_liquor: Clear amber in the black teas, paler and golden in the spring lots.
appearance_wet: Whole, supple leaf with coppery tones in the blacks, greener in the spring teas.
taste_profile: Little consistent tasting detail is documented, as the range varies by style and season. As with other high-altitude Himalayan teas, expect a clean, aromatic cup with floral and fruity notes rather than heavy malt.

brewing.notes: A starting point for the black teas, as is usual for Himalayan leaf. Drop to about 80 C for the green and white lots, and treat season and style as the guide rather than one recipe.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year and season, with the lot name usually stating both: first flush or spring, summer, autumn. Like Darjeeling, the spring teas are for drinking fresh, within a year or so, and summer blacks hold a little longer. Each tea is a named product of a particular year, so one year's lot need not match the next.
description:
Jun Chiyabari, the moonlit tea garden, sits near the small town of Hile in Dhankuta district in eastern Nepal. It is a young garden of about 96 hectares split into five divisions, planted between roughly 1,650 and 2,100 metres or a little higher, and it has become one of the best-known names in Nepali specialty tea.

What sets it apart is the mix of plant material: varietals from India, China, Japan and Taiwan, starting from Darjeeling cultivars, and now a selection of its own called JO. Tea makers decide withering and oxidation by the look, smell and feel of the leaf, and the garden prefers to call its teas high mountain teas instead of orthodox.

The range is wide, so taste depends on the lot. Blacks, greens and whites are named by the garden, and retailers also sell its oolongs. Typical of high Himalayan teas, these lean aromatic and clean more than heavy. Do not brew them all alike: a Western black recipe at slightly lower heat suits the blacks, and greens and whites want cooler water.

Buy by season and year, and read the label closely because product names vary between retailers. The garden works across the oxidation spectrum, so check what style you are getting.
history:
Brothers Bachan and Lochan Gyawali started the garden from nothing in 2001, after scouting sites from early 2000.

It has kept to organic principles, with formal certification in 2012, and it is now moving towards natural farming in the manner of Masanobu Fukuoka.
name_zh: 尼泊尔君奇亚巴里茶园茶
sources_note: Master row had category oolong; the garden profile lists black, green and white only, so set to black. Oolong production not verified. Taste, leaf and liquor text is class-typical. name_zh is a descriptive rendering.
